Learning Objectives
List common postoperative factors affecting recovery after the surgical management of
fractures.
Describe measures to limit postoperative complications in patients with a fracture.
Describe rehabilitation principles to optimize patient recovery after the surgical management
of fractures.
Introduction
Postoperative management is critical to treatment success.
Complications can be limited via preventive measures and early recognition with appropriate
management.

All orthopaedic trauma patients may benefit from physical therapy to restore independence
and functional capacity.

Introduction
Two imperatives are important in the postoperative period: limiting complications and
optimizing recovery. Both are critical as part of a well-executed surgical plan. Limiting
complications includes preventive or prophylactic actions and early recognition and
management for evolving complications. Geriatric co-management is an example of
prophylactic and early management to limit complications.1,2 Optimizing recovery
centers on the restoration of joint mobility and limb function. Critical aspects include
joint range of motion and stability, muscle strength, flexibility, and endurance to allow
for coordinated and complex activity, such as walking, running, and jumping for the
lower extremity and hygiene, feeding, and throwing for the upper extremity. The goal of
rehabilitation for the patient is a return to preinjury level of function via formal physical
therapy or directed individual exercise. Even in the intensive care setting, benefits are
observed with early institution of physical therapy,3 with shortened intensive care unit
and hospital length of stays,4 shorter duration of delirium and mechanical ventilation,
and greater functional independence on discharge5 (Video 1).

Postoperative Complications
Nutrition
Malnutrition may be observed in as many as 50% of hospitalized surgical patients.
Malnutrition is associated with adverse outcomes in trauma patients.
Poor wound healing
Decubitus ulcers
Nonunion
Laboratory evaluation may include the following:
Albumin and prealbumin levels
Total protein level
Transferrin level
Total lymphocyte count
Nutritional supplementation has not been shown to improve outcomes.

Nutrition
Wound and fracture healing require adequate nutrition, including total caloric intake and
ample protein to prevent catabolism that may follow major injury.6 Malnutrition rates
are as high as 50% in hospitalized surgical patients and have been associated with
wound healing problems, decubitus ulcers, and nonunion.7-9 Low vitamin D levels are
common in trauma patients, especially those with increased skin pigmentation.10
Trauma and geriatric patients often are malnourished before the traumatic event. After
injury, nutritional requirements are increased while appetite may be diminished. In
addition, frequent trips to the operating room may require recurring fasting. Such a
scenario may lead to nutritional depletion. To avoid malnourishment, prompt return to
enteral nutrition is important. Providing appetizing food and supplements encourages

adequate nutrition. In a database study of 12,373 patients, severely malnourished hip
fracture patients, defined as those with an albumin level less than 2.4 g/dL (normal ≥3.5
g/dL), had a twofold increase in postoperative complications and mortality;11 however,
few studies on trauma patients have shown definitive changes in outcomes with
nutritional supplementation.12-14
Wound Healing
Surgical and traumatic wound healing depends on the severity of skin and soft-tissue injury
and on patient factors, such as smoking and diabetes mellitus.
Surgical timing and surgical handling of tissues directly affect tissue healing.
Poor wound healing risks infection and recovery.

Wound Healing
Risks for wound healing depend on the degree of trauma to the soft tissues caused by
the injury and surgical management in addition to patient factors and systemic effects15
(Resource 1). The Tscherne classification16 system grades soft-tissue injury in closed
fractures but is subject to interobserver error. The Gustilo-Anderson and the
AO/Orthopaedic Trauma Association classification systems rate soft-tissue injury for
open fractures. Important surgeon and patient factors affect wound healing.
Appropriate timing of surgical management and soft-tissue handling during surgical
management may limit surgically induced trauma to the soft tissues and limit wound
healing problems. Postoperatively, limiting edema and hematoma formation are
important for wounds at risk. Appropriate dressings and splinting may limit tension or
pressure on wounds, promoting healing. Surgical drains help limit hematoma formation
especially in confined areas, such as the hindfoot and ankle. Negative-pressure dressings
may be useful in large exudative wounds but also have been shown to increase
perfusion and oxygen levels in underlying tissues.17 These may be applied for open
fractures and for some patients with closed or open plateau, pilon, and calcaneus
fractures who have a high risk for infection and wound healing complications18 (Tables
1, 2, 3, and 4).

Infection
Signs of infection at site of fracture fixation include the following:
Increasing swelling, erythema, and pain
Wound dehiscence
Prolonged wound drainage
Nonunion or unexpected fracture construct failure

Nonspecific systemic signs of infection include fever and elevated laboratory markers, such as
white blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level.
Deep wound cultures are the current preferred method to establish a diagnosis of deep
infection but may miss fastidious organisms.

Infection
Surgical wounds must be monitored for infection. Superficial and deep postoperative
infections may be observed at any time postoperatively but usually occur within several
days postoperatively. Superficial infections may be indicators of a deep infection,
requiring providers to maintain a high index of suspicion. Prompt evaluation of
increased swelling, erythema, and wound drainage allow for earlier management
(Videos 2 and 3).

practice. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.

Stage 2: superficial skin slough
Stage 3: full-thickness skin loss with exposed subcutaneous fat
Stage 4: full-thickness skin loss with exposed bone or tendon
Unstageable: full-thickness ulcer covered in eschar precluding evaluation of depth


Decubitus Ulcers
Decubitus ulcer or pressure sore formation in the hospital setting is a preventable
complication. A study showed an ulcer prevalence of 20% in trauma patients hospitalized
more than 2 days.19 For patients in the intensive care unit, ulcer rates of more than 50%
have been cited.20
Ulcers are commonly observed in the posterior heel and over the sacrum but can occur
in any location at which sustained pressure compromises perfusion to the skin.
Symptoms such as burning pain over the heel should prompt inspection; however,
ulcers may develop without symptoms. For patients at risk, routine skin inspection is
required. Geriatric patients with limited mobility and poor nutrition have the highest risk,
but ulcers can occur in any patient. Patients with a head injury, patients undergoing
lengthy ventilator management, and patients with a spinal cord injury also have a high
risk. Patients and nursing staff should be taught to shift position periodically to avoid
sustained pressure on any area. Splints and braces must be carefully applied with
appropriate padding. Standard nursing procedures of frequent turning and skin
inspection are essential. In special circumstances, such as prolonged critical care,
malnutrition, high Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II score, and
preexisting ulcer, special pressure-relieving beds are useful.21,22

After diagnosed, pressure and shear must be kept off the area. In stage 2 and above,
dressings may alleviate shear, but pressure also must be relieved with heel-sparing
boots for heel ulcers or deliberate positioning in a semi-decubitus position for sacral
ulcers. Stage 3 and stage 4 ulcers require wound care in addition to the previously
described measures. In more advanced cases, surgical débridement, flap coverage, and
even amputation may be necessary if osteomyelitis occurs.
Pain
In 2010, 50% of opioid deaths were from prescriptions.23
Up to 20% of trauma patients have preinjury use of opiates,24 which is correlated with
prolonged postoperative opioid use.
Poorly controlled pain at discharge is correlated with depression and posttraumatic stress
disorder25 and lower return to work26 at more than 1 year.
A multimodal pain control protocol can reduce narcotic requirements and associated adverse
effects.
Patients being treated for opioid addiction or dependence via methadone or buprenorphine
(suboxone) require additional care because of the agonist/antagonist nature of these agents.

Pain
A great deal have been published on the importance of pain control to aid in patient
recovery while recognizing the risks of overmanagement27,28 (Resource 2). Successful
pain management allows for effective patient mobilization, physical therapy, nutrition,
and rest. Current protocols typically involve multimodal treatment with the use of
NSAIDs, acetaminophen, narcotic agents, gabapentinoids, and topical analgesic
agents.29 Other pharmacologic agents to consider are muscle relaxants (although with
caution with narcotics because of the sedative effects); alpha-2 agonists (clonidine); and
antidepressants, such as amitriptyline and selective serotonin receptor inhibitors, which
may be useful for neuropathic pain and pain interfering with sleep. Pain management in
the immediate postoperative period is particularly critical. Local and regional blocks have

been found to be useful in this setting but should not be used in patients at risk for
compartment syndrome.
NSAIDs have increased in popularity as the opioid epidemic has spread despite concerns
for inhibition of fracture healing. Laboratory and clinical evidence shows greater
inhibition of bone healing with cyclooxygenase-1 inhibitors compared with
cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors in dose-dependent fashion30,31 (Resource 3). Prescription of
short- and/or low-doses of NSAIDs is reasonable to limit use of narcotic agents.
Trauma patients being treated with methadone and buprenorphine are a challenge to
treat in the perioperative period. Methadone is an opioid agonist, whereas
buprenorphine is a partial agonist with a long half-life. The latter may be combined with
naloxone, an opiate blocker, in the commercial form of suboxone. These medications
limit the analgesic effects of narcotic agents in the perioperative period, limiting their
usefulness. In addition, these patients often have higher levels of baseline pain and are
more likely to self-medicate.32 In treating these patients, multimodal therapy is very
important. Methadone is continued, with additional short-acting opiates in used in
combination with other pharmacologic agents and pain management modalities, such as
regional blocks. Buprenorphine, with its longer half-life and partial agonist effects, is
more complex. Various recommendations have been made, ranging from discontinuing
them 72 hours preoperatively and converting to methadone or continuing with divided
doses and higher dosing of short-acting narcotic agents.33-36 Consultation with a pain
specialist is useful. The provider should communicate with the pain clinic to coordinate
ongoing narcotic prescriptions and expectations for recovery from injury (Videos 4 and
5).

Posttraumatic Stress Disorder/Depression
Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, and pain are associated with poorer patient-
reported outcome scores.
In trauma patients, PTSD and depression are common—as high as 25% and 33%,
respectively.37,38
Risk factors include lower education levels and low economic levels.
PTSD symptoms include hyperarousal, avoidance, numbing, and poor sleep.
Depression symptoms include loss of interest and pleasure, difficulty with concentration, and
poor sleep.
Preventive measures include early psychologic and social support.

Posttraumatic Stress Disorder/Depression
Trauma patients have been shown to have higher rates of depression compared with the
general population, with 28% moderate and 13% severe.39 In addition, PTSD may result
from the injury, with 17% to 42% prevalence in trauma patients.40-42 Some symptoms
are mutual to both conditions. Risk factors for PTSD include lower education level,
especially lower than high school level; low level of social support; and living alone.
Because these disorders interfere with effective recovery, surgeons must be vigilant
during the postinjury period to allow for early management. Questionnaires may be
used as screening tools to assess patients.43
If these disorders are present, referral to appropriate psychiatric, psychologic, and social
work services are indicated. In addition to preventive strategies with early social support,
management includes cognitive behavioral therapy methods and eye movement
desensitization and reprocessing. The importance of preventing and managing PTSD,
depression, and pain is highlighted by the poor patient-reported outcomes in patients
with these problems. In a military cohort with mangled limbs, patients with low pain

difference units of population norms, whereas similar patients with more pain who had

Assessment score.44
Missed Injury
Missed injuries occur even after tertiary survey.
Many missed injuries are orthopaedic; some missed injuries are surgical.
An examination and radiographic evaluation are necessary if new clinical symptoms arise or
impaired recovery is observed.

Missed Injury
Missed injuries may occur in as many of 39% of polytrauma patients, and as many as
22% of missed injuries require surgical management and/or result in disability.45 Varying
definitions of missed injury exist, ranging from after the secondary survey to more than
24 hours after admission. In an orthopaedic literature review, 81% of missed injuries
were orthopaedic, and 35% of missed injuries required surgical management.46
Patients who are intubated, have severe head injury, or present with life and limb-
threatening injury that limits or distracts from a complete initial examination are more
likely to have delayed diagnosis of other injuries. A good tertiary survey will identify most
injuries; however, late diagnosis may still occur. Surgeons, therapists, and nurses must
be vigilant and reassess their patients clinically and radiographically if new symptoms or
atypical impediments to recovery are observed. Although late diagnosis of injuries to the
hands and feet are more typical, any part of the musculoskeletal system can be affected.


Thromboembolism
Trauma patients are prone to deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism because
of the local injury and reduced mobility. Those with injuries to the pelvic ring and
acetabulum have a higher risk. Most patients should be treated with some form of deep
vein thrombosis prophylaxis, whether chemical, mechanical, or a combination. No
routine indication for screening studies or vena cava filter placement exists.
Physical Therapy
Determinants of physical therapy needs are injury pattern and management and patient goals
and resources.
Recommendations and limitations for range of motion, weight bearing, strengthening, and
modalities should be communicated.
For injured athletes and workers, sport-specific programs, work simulation, work hardening,
and functional capacity evaluation may be useful.

Physical Therapy
Most patients with musculoskeletal injuries benefit from physical therapy, ranging from
self-directed to formal intensive full-time rehabilitation services. Regimens should be
individualized based on injury patterns, fixation, and patient-specific goals. Prescriptions
should include motion ranges or restrictions to include active or passive motion, weight-
bearing status, and strengthening methods. In each area, parameters for progression
should be specified.47 Particular rehabilitation protocols for individual fracture types are
described in(Resource 4)
In general, periarticular injuries benefit from motion to reduce scarring, stiffness, and
contracture. Ligaments and tendons similarly benefit from a controlled stress
environment to organize collagen along lines of stress, improving their properties.

Motion and controlled tensile loading of ligament, tendon, and muscle help recovery of
mechanical properties of collagen with more mature organization and parallel
organization. In a rabbit Achilles tendon repair model, immobilized tendons regained
only 50% tendon stiffness by 112 days compared with normal stiffness in mobilized
tendons.48 Similarly, motion is known to have salutary effects on articular cartilage in
rabbits.49
Weight Bearing

Weight Bearing
Weight bearing is beneficial in terms of patient independence and functional recovery50
(Resource 5). In addition, weight bearing promotes bone growth. Most diaphyseal
fractures managed via intramedullary devices permit immediate weight bearing. Even
humeral shaft fractures appropriately plated allow for weight-bearing activity. However,
periarticular injuries often require a period of limited–weight bearing to maintain precise
articular reduction. With improvements in fixation techniques, earlier weight bearing in
these patients is being explored. In elderly patients, weight-bearing restrictions are
difficult to maintain. Therefore, weight bearing is not restricted in patients with proximal
femur fractures and increasingly in patients with fractures in other periarticular regions.
Range of Motion

Range of Motion
Although range of motion prescription ideally is unrestricted postoperatively, joint
stability, fracture construct stability, tendon, ligament, and soft-tissue integrity may
impose limits on motion. If any of these is determined to be compromised at the
conclusion of the procedure, limits on motion may be imposed. Restrictions may include
limits within a specified range and also may be specified to be active, active-assisted, or
passive motion. In active motion, patients use their own muscle strength with or without

the assistance of gravity to regain motion. In active-assisted motion, the patient or
therapist may add an additional force to regain motion. In passive motion, the physical
therapist or patient applies the force across the joint to regain motion. This type of
stretching often is useful but potentially places the greatest load across the joint and
related structures, risking their failure. In the acute posttraumatic period, aggressive
passive motion may be associated with pain and construct failure if forceful. Heterotopic
bone also may result. Therefore, it usually is employed after bone, ligament, and tendon
healing has progressed.
Strengthening

Strengthening
Muscle weakness and atrophy occur rapidly with immobilization and bed rest. Early
institution of upright posture and standing help maintain core strength, whereas use of
the extremities promotes extremity strength. In the injured extremity, strengthening can
be performed via various methods: isometric, isotonic, and isokinetic exercises.
Isometric exercise does not require movement of the joint and is used in an immobilized
limb. For example, a patient with a humeral fracture brace may perform co-contractions
to promote humeral alignment and healing and to preserve muscle tone. Isotonic
exercise is performed against uniform resistance, whereas in isokinetic exercise, the rate
of movement is controlled regardless of the force applied. For most trauma applications,
the distinction between isotonic exercise and isokinetic exercise is not critical; however,
weight-bearing exercise and closed kinetic chain activity promote balance, core strength,
and muscle strengthening.
Modalities

Modalities

Cold therapies decrease acute posttraumatic edema and provide analgesia. Later in the
therapeutic course, thermotherapy or heat therapy may aid in mobilization of stiff joints
and muscles. Electrical stimulation therapy can reduce pain and promote neuromuscular
reeducation. For pain control, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation relies on
stimulation of a complex neuronal network to reduce pain. Transcutaneous electrical
nerve stimulation may be useful in hyperalgesic situations after trauma in subacute and
chronic settings. Neuromuscular reeducation is used to restore muscle strength by
stimulating motor nerves with alternating current, inducing contraction. Although
positive effects have been observed with therapeutic modalities after knee ligament
surgery, no effect has been observed after knee arthroplasty, and a paucity of studies
are available on the effectiveness of therapeutic modalities in the trauma population51
(Resource 6).
Contracture

Contracture
Contracture may occur in the upper or lower extremity. Periarticular fractures, especially
those around the knee, elbow, and ankle are prone to contracture.52 Equinus
contractures of the ankle are not uncommon.
Fracture fixation should aim to allow for early motion to minimize this risk. Splinting in a
functional position rather than in a position of greatest comfort also may preclude later
functional compromise. For example, splinting the ankle in a plantigrade position rather
than equinus will facilitate later standing. Similarly, not allowing the knee to remain
flexed over a pillow for comfort postoperatively helps prevent knee flexion contractures
that make standing and walking more difficult. However, severe comminution,
osteoporosis, and associated soft-tissue conditions may place limits on motion. In
addition, pain and poor patient compliance may promote immobility and contracture.
In addition to secure fixation, engagement of patients, nurses, and physical therapists is
critical to limit the risk of contracture formation. Appropriate splinting can support joints

and limit pain in the early postoperative period. Educating patients and their families
make them active participants in their recovery. In more complex cases, closely
monitored physical therapy allows for controlled motion to limit the risk of contracture.
After a contracture is established, a formal stretching program of passive motion may be
required. In addition, serial static cast or brace immobilization may be used. Dynamic
bracing with spring-loaded or turn-buckle hinges also has been used with variable
success. In refractory cases, surgical release may be required.
Special Clinical Cases
Athletes and Workers

Athletes and Workers
Athletes and workers, especially laborers, may have special requirements to return to
their previous level of activity. In such situations, close communication with the patient
and physical therapist helps establish realistic goals and physical therapy programs. For
workers, this may require work simulation so that they can regain confidence in their
abilities to return to the rigorous physical demands of the work site. Climbing ladders or
carrying loads are examples of skills not routinely performed in physical therapy that
may be required on the job site. In addition, the patient and the physical therapist may
require the development of adaptative skills, postures, and tools to allow for safe and
effective return to work. Work hardening is a physical therapy regimen used to develop
the strength and endurance to complete a full workday. Finally, if residual functional
deficits are present after recovery, a functional capacity evaluation performed by a
physical therapist helps quantify abilities and deficits.

Neurologic Injury: Head and Spinal Cord Injury, Major Nerve Injury
Neurologic Injury: Head and Spinal Cord Injury, Major Nerve Injury
Patients with a head injury present a particular challenge in recovery. The initial injury
may range from mild concussive symptoms to profound coma with dilated pupils and
posturing. Recovery is difficult to predict, ranging from minimal to no cognitive
impairments to a permanent vegetative state. Although advancing age and structural
brain tissue damage lessen the probability of functional recovery, predictions are
imperfect. Management should focus on limiting sequelae while presuming recovery.
Maintaining motion of joints to minimize contracture ultimately will promote standing,
walking, and functional use of the upper extremity. In patients with severe injury,
avoiding contractures that make toileting and other nursing care difficult also is
important.
Spinal cord injuries are more commonly permanent but also require care of extremity
injury. Patients who likely will become wheelchair-bound may benefit from stable and
well-aligned limbs that are flexible. In these patients, avoiding contractures that make
recumbency and sitting difficult are critical goals.53
In patients with a plexus injury or injury to major motor nerves, contractures are the
principal complication to avoid. A rigorous stretching and splinting program instituted
early in the recovery process can help avoid refractory problems while monitoring for
nerve recovery. If the nerve recovers, the limb is optimized for return to use. In patients
in whom nerve injury becomes permanent, the limb without contracture is the best
setting for secondary procedures, such as tendon transfer, nerve repair or transfer, or
arthrodesis. In patients with impaired neurologic function, whether central, as in
patients with a head injury or spinal cord injury, or peripheral, as in patients with a
peripheral nerve injury, the interruption of normal motor and sensory function is
associated with decubitus ulcer formation, which must be actively prevented and
monitored.
